notes: Research-supplied targets (replaces data-seed/targets.json; keeps all its keys). General wellness information, not medical advice. Values are given per kg where the source gives them per kg; 'forProfile' blocks are computed for the current profile (male, 45 y, 90.7 kg / 200 lb, 183 cm) ONLY as a reference. The app should recompute every per-kg value from the latest logged weight (or profile weight). Thresholds marked 'app rule' are design choices, not validated cutoffs.

protein.text: Spread protein across meals, about 20-40 g each, from fish, beans and lentils, eggs, Greek yogurt or chicken.
protein.notes: Daily range is the DGA 2025-2030 protein goal (1.2-1.6 g/kg/day): 1.2 x 90.7 = 108.8 g, 1.6 x 90.7 = 145.1 g (~110-145 g). Per-meal 0.25 g/kg or 20-40 g, evenly spread every 3-4 h, is from the ISSN protein position stand (Jäger 2017), which notes optimal per-dose amounts are 'mixed' and depend on age and recent resistance exercise. ISSN recommends 1.4-2.0 g/kg/day for exercising people; Morton 2018 (meta-analysis of 49 RCTs, resistance training) found no further gain in fat-free mass above ~1.62 g/kg/day, so 1.6 g/kg is used as the field-day aim rather than going higher. These studies are mainly in exercising/resistance-trained adults, so the per-meal spacing is a reasonable but not identical fit for hiking. Phase gate (start after regular eating is established) is an app rule so the target doesn't make meals feel too big.

sources.title: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030 (current edition; supersedes 2020-2025)
Jäger R et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise
Morton RW et al. A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults

sodium.fieldNote: Heavy sweating on field days raises sodium needs, so sodium isn't flagged today.
sodium.notes: Desk days: less than 2,300 mg/day (DGA 2025-2030). DGA 2025-2030 also states 'Highly active individuals may benefit from increased sodium intake to offset sweat losses', but gives no number, so maxMgField is null and field days are not flagged. For scale: the ACSM fluid-replacement position stand (Sawka 2007) reports sweat sodium averaging ~35 mmol/L (range ~10-70 mmol/L), i.e. ~805 mg per liter of sweat (≈230-1,610 mg/L; 1 mmol Na = 23 mg). Losses therefore depend on sweat volume and vary a lot between people; that is why no single field target is given. Highlighting top sodium sources on desk days is an app feature, not a separate guideline.

sources.title: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030 (current edition; supersedes 2020-2025)
American College of Sports Medicine position stand: Exercise and fluid replacement (Sawka MN et al.)

fiber.text: Mostly from whole grains, beans, vegetables, fruit and nuts.

reference.note: Institute of Medicine 2005 Adequate Intake for men 19-50 (14 g per 1,000 kcal). Shown for reference only; the app goal uses the outcome-based Reynolds range.

fiber.notes: Reynolds 2019 (Lancet; series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses of prospective studies and trials): risk reductions across critical outcomes were greatest at 25-29 g/day, and dose-response curves suggested higher intakes may give more benefit, so show '25-29+ g'. DGA 2025-2030 prioritizes fiber-rich whole grains but gives no gram target. Phase 2 only, and paused when SNAQ <= 14 (Wilson 2005 validated cutoff for risk of >=5% weight loss) or when skips for no appetite are logged, because fiber-rich, bulky foods increase fullness and he tends to undereat. The pause is an app rule. Evidence for health benefit is strong; rated moderate here because of that fit caveat.

sources.title: Reynolds A et al. Carbohydrate quality and human health: a series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses
Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030 (current edition; supersedes 2020-2025)
Institute of Medicine (National Academies). Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids (EER equations; PAL categories)

recovery.text: After the hike, have a meal or snack with carbohydrate plus protein, like lentil soup with bread, or yogurt with fruit and oats.
recovery.backToBackText: Another field day within 24 hours: put extra carbohydrate in your recovery meals. Otherwise regular meals are enough.
recovery.notes: Thomas 2016 (AND/DC/ACSM joint position): early recovery (up to ~2 h) protein of 0.25-0.3 g/kg (~15-25 g in typical athletes; 23-27 g for 90.7 kg) with carbohydrate. 'Speedy refuelling' of 1.0-1.2 g/kg/h carbohydrate for the first 4 h is advised only when there are less than 8 h between two fuel-demanding sessions; otherwise normal meals meeting daily fuel needs restore glycogen within ~24 h. The 24-hour 'back-to-back' flag is an app rule that shows the general 'extra carbohydrate' text; the rapidRefuel numbers should only show if the next session is within 8 h. Evidence is from athletes; strenuous hiking is a reasonable but not identical application.

sources.title: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement: Nutrition and Athletic Performance
Jäger R et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise

weighIn.how: Same day each week, in the morning, after using the bathroom, similar clothing. Use the smoothed trend, not single readings.
weighIn.notes: Weekly frequency and smoothing are app design choices (no trial sets an optimal weigh-in frequency for this purpose).

weightAlert.text: Your weight trend has dropped more than 5% in 6 months without trying. That's worth a check-in with your doctor.
weightAlert.notes: GLIM consensus (Cederholm 2019) lists non-volitional weight loss >5% within the past 6 months, or >10% beyond 6 months, as a phenotypic criterion for malnutrition. For 90.7 kg, 5% = 4.5 kg (~10 lb). A weight-loss criterion alone is not a diagnosis (GLIM also requires an etiologic criterion such as reduced intake), so the app shows a neutral 'talk with your doctor' note, not a diagnosis. SNAQ <= 14 predicts risk of losing >=5% within 6 months (Wilson 2005) and can be shown alongside. Rated moderate: GLIM is an international expert consensus, widely adopted, not an outcome trial.

sources.title: Cederholm T et al. GLIM criteria for the diagnosis of malnutrition - A consensus report from the global clinical nutrition community
Wilson MM et al. Appetite assessment: simple appetite questionnaire predicts weight loss in community-dwelling adults and nursing home residents

socialEating.text: Low-appetite day? If you can, share a meal: field crew lunch or a family dinner. People tend to eat more with friends or family.
socialEating.notes: Ruddock 2019 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 42 studies): people ate more with friends than alone (SMD 0.76, 95% CI 0.48-1.03); no reliable effect when eating with strangers or acquaintances (SMD 0.21, CI crosses 0). Mostly lab/observational studies; not tested as an intervention for people who undereat. Show only as an optional suggestion on low-appetite days.

sources.title: Ruddock HK et al. A systematic review and meta-analysis of the social facilitation of eating

goalSetting.text: Pick one specific goal for this week. Log it each day; at the end of the week you'll get one line on what went well and what to adjust.
goalSetting.notes: Harkin 2016 (meta-analysis of 138 experimental studies, N=19,951): interventions that increased progress monitoring improved goal attainment (d = 0.40, 95% CI 0.32-0.48), with larger effects when progress was physically recorded or reported to others. Samdal 2017 (meta-regression of 48 studies in adults with overweight/obesity): goal setting and self-monitoring were associated with short- and long-term effects on physical activity and healthy eating. That sample differs from him (obesity), and the 'one goal per week' cap is an app rule matching the slow pace he chose.

sources.title: Harkin B et al. Does monitoring goal progress promote goal attainment? A meta-analysis of the experimental evidence
Samdal GB et al. Effective behaviour change techniques for physical activity and healthy eating in overweight and obese adults; systematic review and meta-regression analyses
